title: LA Schools Pull the Plug: Massive Screen-Time Limits Hit 400,000 Students
summary: The first day of school in Los Angeles came with a dramatic twist: for the first time, students in 1st grade and under are barred from using screens entirely. The policy, passed by the school board this spring, will expand in November to all elementary grades and later to middle and high schools, affecting the district's more than 400,000 students. It's a sharp U-turn for LAUSD, which just a few years ago was a national leader in classroom technology. The new rules have left many educators reeling. "I don't feel like I'm being set up for success," said Armaghan Khan, a science teacher at Johnnie L. Cochran Middle School, who relies on laptops for interactive simulations like car crash physics. He and others say they've received little guidance on how to teach without digital tools. Kirti Baranwal, a librarian at William Jefferson Clinton Middle School with 28 years in the district, supports limits but worries about the void left when screens are removed. Last year, after the district banned cell phones, she asked students to report their own screen time—many logged 8 to 10 hours daily. "I was like, when are you sleeping?" she recalled. Research shows that for kids without access to sports or arts programs, phones often fill their out-of-school hours. The district is treating this as a transitional year. Software on student devices will track weekly screen time without enforcing hard cutoffs, giving administrators data to refine the policy later. Virtual textbooks are exempt, but teachers are still puzzling over where other activities fit. "I have more questions than immediate concerns," Baranwal said. As the school year begins, LAUSD is grappling with a fundamental question: if not screens, then what?
why_it_matters: How schools manage screens shapes how students learn to focus, build real-world skills, and interact with each other, habits that will follow them into adulthood and influence everything from their health to their careers.

background_read: LAUSD, the second-largest school district in the United States serving over 400,000 students in Los Angeles, was once a national pioneer in placing a laptop or tablet in every student's hands. By 2023, many districts had fully adopted 1-to-1 device programs, but a growing body of research began linking excessive screen time to attention problems, sleep disruption, and reduced social interaction in children and teens. In response, several states and school systems across the country started questioning the all-digital approach, with some, like LAUSD, moving to sharply restrict screens during the school day. The district's decision reflects a broader international debate about balancing technology's educational benefits with its potential harms, especially for younger students whose brains are still developing.

perspectives.description: Supporters say reducing screen time at school protects students from digital addiction, eye strain, and the mental health harms linked to constant phone use; it can also encourage more face-to-face collaboration and physical activity.

Many teachers argue the ban was rushed without giving them alternative tools or training, leaving them scrambling to replace interactive science simulations and other effective digital lessons that engaged students who might otherwise struggle.

The shift mirrors a pendulum swing in education policy: after a decade of promoting screens as the future, school systems are now grappling with unintended consequences. The LAUSD 'transitional year' is a careful attempt to gather data before making permanent rules, recognizing that a one-size-fits-all ban may overlook subject-specific needs.

If the data show that certain screen activities (like interactive physics programs) boost learning, LAUSD might carve out exceptions for educational software that research supports, pairing it with clear time limits and better teacher training rather than simply pulling the plug entirely.
